item.title: Re: SCP: The Tooth Jar (seeking greenlights)
item.content:encoded:
Thank you.

My concern with your idea for test logs is that it feels…kinda like they aren't adding much

True, I felt like I had to pitch in logs, since you seemed to want a more story-telling article, but they actually won't add much.

I'm not sure narrowing the list of foods down from 'all foods' to 'some foods' is interesting reading

I agree, this observation doesn't deserve a log. I was thinking more of referring to such test in the SCP effect's description, alluding to the discomfort and possible mouth injuries that the SCP causes.

it feels like you're wanting to keep this short, which'll likely make evocative tooth writing hard

I don't feel like that would be an issue. But it does not have to be an excessively short article to the point I can't convey the ideas.

I'm a little unclear also on why the coins are radioactive?

It's only a small detail. It would be hypothetized in the article that this is linked to the transmutation, which happens at the atomic stage.

it's kinda missing that bit right at the end where a reader goes from 'ew that's weird' to 'oh god what the fuck', y'know? It feels like it needs just, a final way to extrapolate this from 'creates teeth in your food that you can exchange for money' into a horrifying conclusion?

I see what you mean. I didn't think all SCPs required a horryfing bit. I can think of something :
how about subjects exposed to this SCP start developping an unhealthy fascination for teeth, ranging from inspecting their smile in the mirror several times per day and increased dental hygiene at a minimal exposure, to wanting to tear off their own teeth to place them in the SCP at the most extreme exposure.
Subjects strongly influenced by the SCP would want to collect as many coins as possible from the SCP.

What do you think of this?

item.title: Re: SCP: The Tooth Jar (seeking greenlights)
item.content:encoded:
My concern with your idea for test logs is that it feels…kinda like they aren't adding much we don't get a mental picture of from the description of the SCP? Like, I'm not sure narrowing the list of foods down from 'all foods' to 'some foods' is interesting reading, and it feels like you're wanting to keep this short, which'll likely make evocative tooth writing hard?

I'm a little unclear also on why the coins are radioactive? It feels like detail you've added to really explain why this isn't good but it feels…like a weird bit tacked on at the end rather than the natural conclusion of what came before.

To be honest: this feels like an article that would work in the same vein as e.g. SCP-3794 but it feels like it's kinda missing that bit right at the end where a reader goes from 'ew that's weird' to 'oh god what the fuck', y'know? It feels like it needs just, a final way to extrapolate this from 'creates teeth in your food that you can exchange for money' into a horrifying conclusion? Or perhaps a subtle horror would work too: like the article hints at the radiation excuse being so the foundation can quickly claim all the coins and there's like a suggestion they're actively ensuring that people eat in range of this to make money maybe.

item.title: Re: SCP: The Tooth Jar (seeking greenlights)
item.content:encoded:
Thank you for your review. It's very informative.

Indeed, I omitted to present my ideas to build around this SCP, due to wanting to be very thorough with its description.

The article would describe the SCP in the usual objective fashion, complemented with tests to understand its properties :

For example, a log could feature uncomfortable D-classes eating through all sorts of food to test out which trigger teeth apparitions, and subsequently get diagnosed with some bone disease. Then, the article would show studies made about the transmutation, trying to understand exactly what kind of objects gets transmuted (do regular teeth also work?)

The article itself will describe the object's known properties thoroughly and the reader may make the rapprochement with the tooth fairy (but whether they do or do not is not very important).

I think this is enough to make a short article about a fun weird object that is at the same time somewhat cute (turning your fallen teeth into a small payment) and somewhat unsettling (teeth in your food, osteoporosis and radiations). What do you think?

item.title: Re: SCP: The Tooth Jar (seeking greenlights)
item.content:encoded:
My biggest concern with this pitch is you've spent the entire central narrative section talking about 'what does the SCP do' when really what I want to know from there is 'what does the article do with the SCP?'

The core idea here is evocative and I kinda like both it and the idea it's a reimagining of the tooth fairy; but my concern here is…I don't know what you're doing to like,,,show this? I don't know how you're tying the tooth fairy in or what you're going to do to show the unpleasantness here or really anything, y'know?

My feeling is that this idea won't be strong enough to survive if all you do is describe the SCP; and I have some concerns that the idea is narrow to the point where you don't really have much room to tell an interesting story around what it does but I'm also open to being wrong here.

item.title: SCP: The Tooth Jar (seeking greenlights)
item.content:encoded:
Seeking Greenlights: Yes

Page Type: SCP Article

Elevator Pitch:

  • SCP-XXXX is an ordinary looking empty glass jar
  • If a human subject is eating a meal within a short distance radius around SCP-XXXX, teeth will appear inside the food
  • Putting these teeth inside the jar will transmute them into radioactive coins
+ Latest version (22/11/2020)
- Show less

Central Narrative:

SCP-XXXX is a ordinary looking glass jar that can be closed with a metallic lid.

Eating solid food within a 20 meter radius around SCP-XXXX will make the subject bite on a tooth, appearing inside the food. This tooth, called SCP-XXXX-1, matches the DNA of the subject that bit on it, although no loss of tooth is observed on the subject.

This phenomenon can be repeated. Every time an instance of SCP-XXXX-1 is created, its mass is substracted from the subject's bone mass. Excessive repetition of the phenomenon may lead to bone diseases.

Placing instances of SCP-XXXX-1 into SCP-XXXX, closing it with the lid, and breaking all visual contact with it allow for the transmutation event to take place instantly. The transmutation replaces all instances of SCP-XXXX-1 with coins, referred to as SCP-XXXX-2.

Instances of SCP-XXXX-2 look identical to coins of the French Franc currency, melted in 1982. The SCP-XXXX-2 are highly radioactive, warranting their rapid disposal.

The article would describe the SCP in the usual objective fashion, complemented with tests to understand its properties :

For example, a log could feature uncomfortable D-classes eating through all sorts of food to test out which trigger teeth apparitions, and subsequently get diagnosed with some bone disease. Then, the article would show studies made about the transmutation, trying to understand exactly what kind of objects gets transmuted (do regular teeth also work?)

This would be a short article about a fun weird object that is at the same time somewhat cute (turning your fallen teeth into a small payment) and somewhat unsettling (teeth in your food, osteoporosis and radiations)


Hook/Attention-Grabber: Have you ever bitten on your own dislodged tooth while eating, when you were a child? It's not the most pleasant of sensations. This SCP also twists the tale of the tooth fairy in a SCP-esque fashion.
+ Version 1 (21/11/2020)
- Show less

Central Narrative:

SCP-XXXX is a ordinary looking glass jar that can be opened or closed with a metallic lid. Manufacturing codes engraved at the bottom of SCP-XXXX suggest it originally was a jar of Dijon mustard.

Eating solid food within a 20 meter radius around SCP-XXXX will have the following effect occur: after chewing four to five times, the subject will bite on a small human tooth, that was not initially present in the food. This tooth, called SCP-XXXX-1, matches the DNA of the subject that bit on it, although no loss of tooth is observed on the subject.

This phenomenon can be repeated. An instance of SPC-XXXX-1 will appear in the consumed food every four to five mastications, and this will always result in the subject biting onto it, leading to possible mouth injuries if unprepared.
Every time an instance of SCP-XXXX-1 is created, its mass is substracted from the subject's bone mass. Excessive repetition of the phenomenon on the same subject will result in the onset of bone-related diseases, such as osteoporosis.

Placing instances of SCP-XXXX-1 into SCP-XXXX, closing it with the lid, and breaking all visual contact with it allow for the transmutation event to take place instantly.
The transmutation event can occur only if no human person or camera has a visual contact with SCP-XXXX. The transmutation effectively replaces all instances of SCP-XXXX-1 with coins, referred to as SCP-XXXX-2.

Instances of SCP-XXXX-2 look identical to coins of the French Franc currency. Composition and engravings on the surface matches that of regular coins melted in 1982.
All instances of SCP-XXXX-2 are highly radioactive, averaging 80 μSv/h, warranting their rapid disposal.


Hook/Attention-Grabber: Have you ever bitten on your own dislodged tooth while eating, when you were a child? It's not the most pleasant of sensations. This SCP also twists the tale of the tooth fairy in a SCP-esque fashion.
